---
title: "The Bernoulli distribution"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The [preceding page](bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions.qmd) mapped each interrogative argument in the Turkish BOUN extract to an object indicator. The **Bernoulli distribution** describes that single binary measurement.

For a not-yet-sampled token outcome $\omega_i$, define
$O_i(\omega_i)=1$ if its source relation is `obj` and zero if it is `nsubj`.
After observing the row, $o_i$ is the realized zero or one. The model parameter
$p$ is the object probability under a declared sampling process, while
$\widehat p=\sum_i o_i/n$ is its empirical estimate in this extract.

We state the Bernoulli mass function, derive its expectation and variance, and then mark the distinction between a one-draw model and claims about dependence across corpus rows.

```{r}
#| label: load-ud-bernoulli
library(ggplot2)

questions <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
O <- questions$object
p_hat <- mean(O)
bernoulli_pmf <- data.frame(
  object = 0:1,
  count = c(sum(O == 0), sum(O == 1)),
  probability = c(mean(O == 0), mean(O == 1)) # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
)

stopifnot(
  length(O) == 167L,
  all(O %in% 0:1),
  abs(sum(bernoulli_pmf$probability) - 1) < 1e-12,
  abs(mean((O - p_hat)^2) - p_hat * (1 - p_hat)) < 1e-12
)

bernoulli_pmf
```

## Mass, expectation, and variance

For $O\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(O=o)=p^o(1-p)^{1-o}.
$$

Because $O^2=O$, its expectation and variance follow directly:

$$
\mathbb{E}[O]=0(1-p)+1p=p,
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[O]
&=\mathbb{E}[O^2]-\mathbb{E}[O]^2\\
&=p-p^2\\
&=p(1-p).
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the corpus-fitted value gives an expectation of `r sprintf("%.3f", p_hat)` and a variance of `r sprintf("%.3f", p_hat * (1 - p_hat))`. The expectation has an immediate interpretation: it is the empirical proportion of retained interrogative arguments annotated `obj`.

This calculation reuses [expectation as a probability-weighted
average](expected-values.qmd#expectation-as-a-probability-weighted-average) and
[variance as expected squared distance](variance-and-covariance.qmd#variance-as-expected-squared-distance).

```{r}
#| label: plot-ud-bernoulli
#| fig-cap: "Observed Bernoulli mass for subject and object relations in the Turkish BOUN extract."
bernoulli_pmf$relation <- ifelse(bernoulli_pmf$object == 1, "obj", "nsubj")

ggplot(bernoulli_pmf, aes(relation, probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey45", width = 0.65) +
  labs(x = "Annotated dependency relation", y = "Empirical probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## What the model does not say

The fitted $p$ summarizes the retained token table. It does not say that every sentence has the same object probability, nor does it describe repeated independent sampling from Turkish. Sentence and register identifiers remain available because discourse context and sampling structure may matter.

## Check your understanding

1. Verify the identity $\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(O)=\widehat p(1-\widehat p)$ from the individual rows.
2. Compute the empirical Bernoulli PMF for the indicator `lemma == "ne"`.
3. What linguistic distinction does the current zero value encode?
4. Why is $\mathbb{E}[O]$ both a mean and a proportion?
5. Which of $O_i$, $o_i$, $p$, and $\widehat p$ remains random before one token
   is observed, and which is computed from all observed rows?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The row-level indicator variance is $\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}[O]=0.212127$, equal to $\widehat p(1-\widehat p)=0.694611(0.305389)$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. For the *ne* indicator, $p(0)=20/167=0.119760$ and $p(1)=147/167=0.880240$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. For the object indicator $O$, zero encodes the linguistic alternative `nsubj` rather than an absence of data. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. $\mathbb{E}[O]=0\,p_O(0)+1\,p_O(1)=p_O(1)$, which is both the sample mean of the zero-one values and the proportion of object tokens. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. $O_i$ is the random variable and $o_i$ its realization; $p$ is the model
   parameter, while $\widehat p$ is the statistic computed from the realized
   rows.

</details>

Keeping the random indicator, observed value, parameter, and estimate distinct
allows the Bernoulli mean and variance to follow directly from the two-point
PMF. The [binomial distribution](binomial-distribution.qmd) next describes the
count obtained by summing fixed-$n$ iid Bernoulli variables.
